title: CheckMate: Watermarking Graph Diffusion Models
one_liner: Embed watermarks into graph eigenvectors (numbers that don't change if you relabel the graph) so you can verify ownership even if someone modifies the graph.
lead: Imagine you generate a graph (a network of connected dots) using an AI model, and you want to prove later that you created it. A watermark is a hidden fingerprint. The tricky part: graphs can look different but be mathematically identical (if you just relabel the dots), so old watermarking tricks fail. CheckMate embeds the watermark into eigenvalues—special numbers that stay the same no matter how you relabel—making verification fast and unbreakable.

problem.h2: Why is watermarking graphs so hard?
paras: Watermarking is a way to secretly hide your name inside something you created, so you can prove ownership later. Old methods add a hidden marking to the graph after it is generated—say, flipping the color of certain dots or edges. But this ruins the graph quality.

A newer idea: embed the watermark during generation, while the model is still guessing at the structure. This works for images (they are just grids of pixels) but fails for graphs, because two graphs can be identical even if the dots are numbered differently. When someone relabels the dots, the old watermark vanishes. Plus, the graph generation process (diffusion) is extremely hard to reverse, so you cannot easily pull out what was hidden.

callout.html: Old watermarks change when the graph is relabeled, and reversing the generation process is computationally impossible.

steps.text: Model learns to generate graphs by gradually replacing noise with structure.
Before generation starts, secretly set certain eigenvalues to a checkerboard pattern.
Diffusion process builds the graph around the hidden eigenvalue pattern.
Use eigenvectors to map the final discrete graph back to continuous numbers.
Check if the checkerboard pattern exists. If yes, you own this graph.

paras: The paper places the watermark into eigenvalues—special numbers that describe the graph's structure and stay the same even if you relabel all the dots. This is different from marking individual dots or edges, which disappear after relabeling.

hidden.name: eigenvalue signature pattern
paras: Eigenvalues are a set of special numbers that come from the graph's structure. If you arrange the dots of a graph into a matrix (rows and columns), eigenvalues are the magical numbers that tell you how that matrix stretches space. The important fact: eigenvalues are isomorphism-invariant—they stay exactly the same even if you relabel the dots (that is what isomorphism means: the graph is the same, just drawn differently).

CheckMate embeds a checkerboard pattern into these eigenvalues. When the diffusion model generates the graph, it keeps those eigenvalues fixed. To detect the watermark later, the paper reverses the diffusion process, pulls out the eigenvalues, and checks if the checkerboard is still there. Since eigenvalues do not change with relabeling, the watermark survives attacks.

heat.caption: Darker eigenvalues carry the checkerboard watermark. Light ones are ordinary.

reads.html: Eigenvalues are like the DNA of a graph—they tell you its shape. If you rename the dots, the DNA does not change, so the watermark stays hidden in the DNA.
The paper uses eigenvalue-based watermarking because eigenvalues do not change when you relabel the dots, so the watermark survives attacks that rename the graph.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the reversal trick
paras: The diffusion model generates graphs by slowly replacing random noise with structure. The watermark is embedded into eigenvalues before this process starts. Because eigenvalues are isomorphism-invariant, the watermark survives the entire generation process intact.

To find the watermark, you need to reverse the diffusion—pull out what was hidden in the noise. This is normally impossible (the discrete final graph has been rounded from continuous numbers). CheckMate uses eigenvectors (the partners of eigenvalues) to approximately undo that rounding. In plain terms: eigenvectors act like a decoder, translating the final discrete graph back into continuous space where the eigenvalues are readable. Since the watermark lives in the eigenvalues (which do not change under relabeling), it survives even after attackers modify the graph by adding or removing edges.

math.words: For each eigenvalue lambda in the watermark set, check whether it matches the expected checkerboard pattern. The pattern alternates high and low values in a checkerboard order.

charts.title: CheckMate (this paper)
charts.note: Watermark is embedded during generation, maintains quality, and survives all attacks.

items.html: If the diffusion process happens to produce eigenvalues close to the watermark pattern by accident, false positives occur. Mitigated by using a strong threshold and random checkerboard seeding.

Reversing the diffusion is approximate, not exact. Rounding errors when converting the discrete graph back to continuous space can blur the watermark. CheckMate uses sparsification—dropping less-important connections—to make the watermark easier to see through the noise.

If an attacker carefully crafts a graph that preserves utility but scrambles the eigenvalues, the watermark may be destroyed. The paper tests relabeling and edge edits but not all possible adversarial schemes.
Use a unique, random checkerboard pattern for each graph, combine multiple eigenvalue checks, and test with real data to ensure the watermark stays hidden on each new type of graph.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate a graph using a diffusion model trained with CheckMate watermarking. Then verify the watermark is present. Modify the graph by relabeling the dots (isomorphism) and/or by randomly deleting 10-20% of edges. Re-run watermark detection. The watermark should persist.
demo.closing: The demo must show that detection rate stays above 90% even after graph relabeling, while old methods drop to near 0%.
